newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe industry slams South Africa for unfair trade.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe industry slams South Africa for unfair trade.

text.p: Zimbabwean industry leaders on Thursday renewed calls for retaliatory tariff measures against South Africa, accusing it of footdragging in negotiations on a new preferential trade pact between the two countries.
Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) president Jonee Blanchfield said prospects of Harare and Pretoria concluding a new trade agreement by the end of the year had now vanished.

She blamed white South African industrialists in particular for holding the negotiations up, saying they were happy with the current situation under which their goods entered the Zimbabwean market at lower duties while their market was closed to the Zimbabweans due to higher import tariffs.

"For the past four years, we have been told that a new trade pact is imminent. Where is the agreement? They (Zimbabwe and South Africa) have not signed it because of South Africa's delaying tactics," Blanchefield told Reuters.
Zimbabwe and South Africa, southern Africa's biggest trading partners, have engaged in on-off talks on a new trade deal since 1992 when a 1964 preferential pact lapsed.
Serious negotiations only started early this year after Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe threatened his government would retaliate against South Africa.
"The government should now implement countervailing measures against South Africa because while the South Africans are dragging their feet on negotiations, we are suffering here," Blanchefield said.
"Our apples are attracting 30 percent duty in South Africa, so why shouldn't we also levy 30 percent duty on their apples?" asked Blanchefield.
Blanchefield said 31 Zimbabwean clothing and textile firms had closed down in the past 18 months after South Africa slapped duties of up to 90 percent on their goods to protect its industry.
However, deputy industry and commerce minister Obert Moyo said the government believed on-going negotiations between the two countries would be concluded soon.
"We don't feel we should impose retaliatory measures against South Africa yet. Negotiations are still on course and we are hopeful there will be a positive outcome soon," he told Reuters.

Earlier on Thursday, Mpofu told a CZI seminar that cabinet would meet next Tuesday to consider revisions to new protective tariffs which were introduced on July 1 but were withdrawn a week later because the government said it had not consulted widely.
The country's leading battery manufacturer, Chloride, urged the government to re-introduce the new structure quickly to protect the local battery industry from cheaper imports from South Africa.
Mpofu could not be drawn into saying when the revised tariffs would be effective.
